chung.Description:
1. Course Objectives:

This application-based course provides undergraduate students with a strong foundation of business data analytics, focusing on data visualization, multiple regression, data mining, linear optimization models, simulation, and decision analysis, while enabling students to gain familiarity and develop mastery of these topics within the contexts of big data and artificial intelligence.

2. Course Content:

Key topics include: Data Visualisation; Descriptive Analysis; Linear Regression; Predictive Data Mining and Analysis; Optimization; Big Data Analytics.

3. Activities and Teaching Methodology:

Lectures, hands-on coding sessions, and individual and group projects will help students practice and develop fundamental data management and analysis techniques using Python, R, and Excel, while also exploring their application in the contexts of big data and AI to address complex, large-scale business challenges.

clo: Explain the role of business analytics in business and financial decision-making, including analytics processes, data types, data sources, big-data/AI contexts, and basic ethical/privacy considerations.

Prepare business or financial datasets for analysis by applying foundational data-handling skills from BCP201, including importing, inspecting, cleaning, transforming, joining, and documenting data using guided tools such as Excel, Python, or R.
Apply descriptive analytics and data visualization techniques to summarize business data, identify basic patterns or outliers, and communicate insights clearly to non-technical stakeholders.

Apply introductory statistical and predictive analytics methods, including basic inference, regression, forecasting, and selected classification or data-mining techniques, to support business or financial decisions.

Use introductory prescriptive analytics tools, including spreadsheet decision models, what-if analysis, simulation, and basic linear/integer optimization, to evaluate alternatives under constraints and uncertainty.

Complete a guided end-to-end business analytics project, individually and/or in teams, by framing a business problem, preparing data, selecting suitable introductory methods, interpreting results responsibly, and presenting evidence-based recommendations.
danhGia: Group project: dataset-based analysis, report/slides, presentation, and Q&A using rubric criteria

End-to-end business analytics project: problem framing; data preparation; descriptive/visual analysis; one suitable introductory predictive or prescriptive method; limitations; evidence-based recommendation. Groups may use Excel, Python, or R where feasible, but advanced data-mining methods and complex coding are optional/awareness-level only and should not be required.

Groups complete a guided project using an approved dataset and present findings. The project should demonstrate usable business reasoning, clear communication, and explainable tool/method choices rather than technical complexity. Any Excel/Python/R outputs used must be interpreted in non-technical business language.

Introduced in Session 3, checked around Session 42, finalized around Session 54, and presented in Sessions 58-59. Recommend keeping supporting materials to a project brief, rubric, and presentation guidance only.

Data preparation, descriptive statistics, visualization, and one introductory inferential or predictive analysis selected from the covered topics. Students may use appropriate guided tools such as Excel, Python, or R, but the expected level is business interpretation, not complex coding, advanced modeling, or advanced specific programming.

Students work individually on a provided or lecturer-approved dataset. They submit a concise analytics output/report explaining data preparation decisions, selected method, key results, limitations, and a business recommendation. Outputs may come from Excel, Python, R, or prepared/guided workflows, provided the student can interpret them correctly.

Introduced in Session 9, supported through consultation/checkpoints, and aligned with the submission/feedback window around Sessions 30-33. The task should remain compact enough for a midterm-style take-home assessment. Do not require advanced R use as mandatory; allow it only as one feasible tool option.

Students participate in guided exercises, answer short in-class questions, discuss cases, and complete selected low-stakes tasks using the course dataset pack. The focus is engagement, interpretation, and learning process, not advanced coding performance or syntax memorization.
